div2.head: [Scene 1]
div2.stage: Enter the Count Labervele in his shirt and night-gown with two jewels in his hand.

lg.l: Yet hath the morning sprinkled thr’out the clouds
But half her tincture, and the soil of night
Sticks still upon the bosom of the air.
Yet sleep doth rest my love for nature’s debt,
And through her window and this dim twilight
Her maid, nor any waking I can see.
This is the holy green, my wife’s close walk,
— To which not any but herself alone
Hath any key, only that I have clapped
Her key in wax and made this counterfeit —
To the which I steal access
To work this rare and politic device.
Fair is my wife, and young and delicate,
Although too religious in the purist sort;
But pure religion being but mental stuff,
And sense, indeed, all for itself,
Is to be doubted; that, when an object comes
Fit to her humour, she will intercept
Religious letters sent unto her mind,
And yield unto the motion of her blood.
Here have I brought, then, two rich agates for her,
Graven with two posies of mine own devising,
For poets I’ll not trust, nor friends, nor any.
She longs to have a child, which yet, alas,
I cannot get, yet long as much as she,
And not to make her desperate, thus I write
In this fair jewel, though it simple be,
Yet ’tis mine own, that meaneth well enough:
Despair not of children,
Love with the longest;
When man is at the weakest,
God is at the strongest.
I hope ’tis plain and knowing. In this other, that I write:
God will reward her a thousandfold
That takes what age can, and not what age would.
I hope ’tis pretty and pathetical.
Well, even here
Lie both together till my love arise
And let her think you fall out of the skies.
I will to bed again.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: How like thou this morning, Colinet? What, shall we have a fair day?

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: The sky hangs full of humour, and I think we shall have rain.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, rain is fair weather when the ground is dry and barren, especially when it rains humour, for then do men like hot sparrows and pigeons open all their wings ready to receive them.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Why, then, we may chance to have a fair day, for we shall spend it with so humorous acquaintance as rains nothing but humour all their lifetime.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: True, Colinet, over which will I sit like an old king in an old-fashion play, having his wife, his council, his children, and his fool about him, to whom he will sit and point very learnedly as followeth:

lg.l: My council grave, and you my noble peers,
My tender wife, and you my children dear,
And thou my fool —

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Not meaning me, sir, I hope.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: No, sir, but thus will I sit, as it were, and point out all my humorous companions.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: You shall do marvellous well, sir.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I thank you for your good encouragement. But, Colinet, thou shalt see Catalian bring me hither an odd gentleman presently to be acquainted withal, who in his manner of taking acquaintance will make us excellent sport.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Why, Lemot, I think thou sendest about of purpose for young gallants to be acquainted withal, to make thyself merry in the manner of taking acquaintance.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: By heaven I do, Colinet, for there is no better sport than to observe the complement, for that’s their word, complement, do you mark, sir?

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Yea, sir, but what humour hath this gallant in his manner of taking acquaintance?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Marry thus, sir: he will speak the very selfsame word to a syllable after him of whom he takes acquaintance, as if I should say, ‘I am marvellous glad of your acquaintance’, he will reply, ‘I am marvellous glad of your acquaintance’. ‘I have heard much good of your rare parts and fine carriage’; ‘I have heard much good of your rare parts and fine carriage’. So long as the complements of a gentleman last, he is your complete ape.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Why, this is excellent.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Nay, sirrah, here’s the jest of it: when he is past this gratulation, he will retire himself to a chimney or a wall standing folding his arms thus; and go you and speak to him so far as the room you are in will afford you, you shall never get him from that most gentlemanlike set or behaviour.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: This makes his humour perfect. I would he would come once.

p.seg: See where he comes. Now must I say, Lupus est in fabula , for these Latin ends are part of a gentleman and a good scholar.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Oh, good morrow Monsieur Lemot. Here is the gentleman you desired so much to be acquainted withal.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: He is marvellous welcome. [To Blanvel] I shall be exceeding proud of your acquaintance.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: I shall be exceeding proud of your acquaintance.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I have heard much good of your rare parts and fine carriages.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: I have heard much good of your rare parts and fine carriages.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I shall be glad to be commanded by you.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: I shall be glad to be commanded by you.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I pray do not you say so.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: I pray do not you say so.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well, gentlemen, this day let’s consecrate to mirth. And Colinet, you know, no man better, that you are mightily in love with lovely Martia, daughter to old Foyes.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: I confess it. Here are none but friends.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well then, go to her this morning in Countess Moren’s name, and so perhaps you may get her company, though the old churl be so jealous that he will suffer no man to come at her but the vain gull Labesha for his living sake, and he, as yet, she will not be acquainted withal.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Well, this I’ll do, whatsoever come on it.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why nothing but good will come of it, ne’er doubt it man.

p.seg: He hath taken up his stand. Talk a little further and see an you can remove him.
I will, Catalian.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: I do, sir, very well, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: You know the old Count Labervele hath a passing fair young lady, that is a passing foul Puritan?

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: I know her very well, sir. She goes more like a milkmaid than a countess, for all her youth and beauty.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: True, sir. Yet of her is the old Count so jealous that he will suffer no man to come at her. Yet I will find a means that two of us will have access to her, though before his face, which shall so heat his jealous humour till he be stark mad. But, Colinet, go you first to lovely Martia, for ’tis too soon for the old lord and his fair young lady to rise.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Adieu , Monsieur Blanvel.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Adieu , good Monsieur Colinet.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Monsieur Blanvel, your kindness in this will bind me much to you.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Monsieur Lemot, your kindness in this will bind me much to you.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I pray you do not say so, sir.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: I pray you do not say so sir.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Will’t please you to go in?

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Will’t please you to go in?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I will follow you.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: I will follow you.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: It shall be yours.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: It shall be yours.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Kind Monsieur Blanvel.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Kind Monsieur Lemot.

div2.head: [Scene 3]
div2.stage: Enter Foyes and Martia and Labesha.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: Come on, fair daughter, fall to your work of mind, and make your body fit to embrace the body of this gentleman’s, ’tis art: happy are they, say I.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: I protest, sir, you speak the best that ever I heard.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: I pray, sir, take acquaintance of my daughter.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: I do desire you of more acquaintance.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: [To Martia] Why dost not thou say ‘Yea, and I the same of you’?

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: That everybody says.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: Oh, you would be singular.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Single, indeed.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: ‘Single, indeed’: that’s a pretty toy! Your betters, dame, bear double, and so shall you.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Exceeding pretty, did you mark it, forsooth?

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: What should I mark, forsooth?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Your bearing double, which equivocate is, and hath a fit allusion to a horse that bears double, for your good father means you shall endure your single life no longer, not in worse sense than bearing double, forsooth.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: I cry you mercy, you know both belike.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Knowledge, forsooth, is like a horse and you, that can bear double. It nourisheth both bee and spider: the bee honeysuckle, the spider, poison. I am that bee.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: I thought so by your stinging wit.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Lady, I am a bee without a sting, no way hurting any, but good to all, and before all, to your sweet self.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: Afore God, daughter, thou art not worthy to hear him speake. But who comes here?

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: God save you, sir.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: You are welcome, sir, for aught that I know yet.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: I hope I shall be so still, sir.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: What is your business, sir, and then I’ll tell you?

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Marry thus, sir, the Countess Moren entreats your fair daughter to bear her company this forenoon.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: This forenoon, sir? Doth my lord or lady send for her, I pray?

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: My lady, I assure you.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: My lady, you assure me. Very well, sir. Yet that house is full of gallant gentlemen, dangerous thorns to prick young maids, I can tell you.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: There are none but honest and honourable gentlemen.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: All is one, sir, for that. I’ll trust my daughter with any man, but no man with my daughter, only yourself Monsieur Besha, whom I will entreat to be her guardian and to bring her home again.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: I will wait upon her, an it please you.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: No, sir, your weight upon her will not be so good. Here, Monsieur Besha, I deliver my daughter unto you a perfect maid, and so I pray you look well unto her.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Farewell, Monsieur Foyes.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: I warrant I’ll look unto her well enough. Mistress, will it please you to preambulate.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: With all my heart.

lg.l: What have I done? Put on too many clothes.
The day is hot, and I am hotter clad
Than might suffice health.
My conscience tells me that I have offended,
And I’ll put them off.
That will ask time that might be better spent.
One sin will draw another quickly so.
See how the Devil tempts. But what’s here?
Jewels?
How should these come here?
Good morrow, lovely wife. What hast thou there?
Jewels, my lord, which here I strangely found.
That’s strange indeed. What, where none comes
But when yourself is here? Surely the heavens
Have rained thee jewels for thy holy life,
And using thy old husband lovingly,
Or else do fairies haunt this holy green,
As evermore mine ancestors have thought.
Fairies were but in times of ignorance,
Not since the true pure light hath been revealed.
And that they come from heaven I scarce believe.
For jewels are vain things. Much gold is given
For such fantastical and fruitless jewels,
And therefore heaven, I know, will not maintain
The use of vanity. Surely I fear
I have much sinned to stoop and take them up,
Bowing my body to an idle work.
The strength that I have had to this very deed
Might have been used to take a poor soul up
In the highway.
You are too curious, wife. Behold your jewels.
What, methinks there’s posies written on them.
Despair not of children,
Love with the longest;
When man is at the weakest,
God is at the strongest.
Wonderful rare and witty, nay, divine.
Why, this is heavenly comfort for thee, wife.
What is this other?
God will reward her a thousandfold
That takes what age can, and not what age would.
The best that ever I heard. No mortal brain,
I think, did ever utter such conceit
For good plain matter and for honest rhyme.
Vain poetry. I pray you burn them, sir.
You are to blame, wife. Heaven hath sent you them
To deck yourself withal, like to yourself,
Not to go thus like a milkmaid.
Why there is difference in all estates
By all religion.
There is no difference.
I prithee, wife, be of another mind
And wear these jewels and a velvet hood.
A velvet hood! O vain devilish device!
A toy made with a superfluous flap,
Which being cut off, my head were still as warm.
Diogenes did cast away his dish
Because his hand would serve to help him drink.
Surely these heathens shall rise up against us.
Sure, wife, I think thy keeping always close,
Making thee melancholy, is the cause
We have no children, and therefore, if thou wilt,
Be merry and keep company i’ God’s name.
Sure, my lord, if I thought I should be rid
Of this same banishment of barrenness,
And use our marriage to the end it was made,
Which was for procreation, I should sin,
If by my keeping house I should neglect
The lawful means to be a fruitful mother;
And therefore if it please you I’ll use resort.

p.seg: God’s my passion, what have I done? Who would have thought her pureness would yield so soon to courses of temptations?

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: I know, my lord, ’tis true, but the lawful means must still be used.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Yea, the lawful means indeed must still, but now I remember that lawful means is not abroad.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Well, well, I’ll keep the house still.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Nay, hark you, lady, I would not have you think — marry, I must tell you this, if you should change the manner of your life, the world would think you changed religion too.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: ’Tis true, I will not go.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Nay, if you have a fancy.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Yea, a fancy, but that’s no matter.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Indeed, fancies are not for judicial and religious women.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: God save your lordship, and you, most religious lady.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Sir, you may say God save us well indeed That thus are thrust upon in private walks.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: A slender thrust, sir, where I touched you not.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Well, sir, what is your business?

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Why, sir, I have a message to my lady from Monsieur du Barte.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: To ‘your lady’? Well, sir, speak your mind to ‘your lady’.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: You are very welcome, sir, and I pray how doth he?

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: In health, madam, thanks be to God, commending his duty to your ladyship, and hath sent you a message which I would desire your honour to hear in private.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: ‘My ladyship’, and ‘my honor’! They be words which I must have you leave. They be idle words, and you shall answer for them truly. ‘My duty to you’, or ‘I desire you’, were a great deal better than ‘my ladyship’, or ‘my honour’.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: I thank you for your Christian admonition.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Nay, thank God for me. Come, I will hear your message with all my heart, and you are very welcome, sir.

p.seg: ‘With all my heart, and you are very welcome, sir’, and go and talk with a young lusty fellow able to make a man’s hair stand upright on his head! What purity is there in this, trow you? Ha, what wench of the faculty could have been more forward? Well, sir, I will know your message.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Why you shall, sir, if you be so desirous.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Nay, sir, I am more than so desirous. Come, sir, study not for a new device now.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Not I, my lord, this is both new and old. I am a scholar, and being spiritually inclined by your lady’s most godly life, I am to profess the ministry and to become her chaplain, to which end Monsieur du Barte hath commended me.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Her chaplain, in the Devil’s name, fit to be vicar of hell!

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: My good head, what are you afraid of? He comes with a godly and neighbourly suit. What, think you his words or his looks can tempt me? Have you so little faith? If every word he spake were a serpent as subtle as that which tempted Eve, he cannot tempt me, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Well answered for him, lady, by my faith. Well, hark you, I’ll keep your chaplain’s place yonder for a while, and at length put in one myself. (Enter Lemot. ) What, more yet? God’s my passion, whom do I see? The very imp of desolation, the minion of our King, whom no man sees to enter his house but he locks up his wife, his children, and his maids, for where he goes he carries his house upon his head like a snail. Now, sir, I hope your business is to me.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: No, sir, I must crave a word with my lady.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: These words are intolerable, and she shall hear no more.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: She must hear me speak.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Must she, sir? Have you brought the King’s warrant for it?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I have brought that which is above kings.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Why, every man for her sake is a Puritan. The Devil I think will shortly turn Puritan, or the Puritan will turn devil.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: What have you brought, sir?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Marry this, madam. You know we ought to prove one another’s constancy, and I am come in all chaste and honourable sort to prove your constancy.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: You are very welcome, sir, and I will abide your proof. It is my duty to abide your proof.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: You’ll bide his proof? It is your duty to bide his proof! How the devil will you bide his proof?

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: My good head, no otherwise than before your face in all honourable and religious sort. I tell you I am constant to you, and he comes to try whether I be so or no, which I must endure. Begin your proof, sir.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Nay, madam, not in your husband’s hearing, though in his sight, for there is no woman will show she is tempted from her constancy, though she be a little. Withdraw yourself, sweet lady.

p.seg: Well, I will see though I do not hear. Women may be courted without offence, so they resist the courtier.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Dear and most beautiful lady, of all the sweet honest and honourable means to prove the purity of a lady’s constancy, kisses are the strongest. I will therefore be bold to begin my proof with a kiss.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: No, sir, no kissing.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: No kissing, madam? How shall I prove you then sufficiently not using the most sufficient proof? To flatter yourself by affection of spirit, when it is not perfectly tried, is sin.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: You say well, sir. That which is truth is truth.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Then do you well, lady, and yield to the truth.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: By your leave, sir, my husband sees. Peradventure it may breed an offence to him.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: How can it breed an offence to your husband to see your constancy perfectly tried?

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: You are an odd man, I see. But first, I pray, tell me how kissing is the best proof of chaste ladies.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: To give you a reason for that, you must give me leave to be obscure and philosophical.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: I pray you be. I love philosophy well.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Then thus, madam: every kiss is made, as the voice is, by imagination and appetite, and as both those are presented to the ear in the voice, so are they to the silent spirits in our kisses.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: To what spirit mean you?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: To the spirits of our blood.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: What if it do?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why then, my imagination and mine appetite working upon your ears in my voice, and upon your spirits in my kisses, piercing therein the more deeply, they give the stronger assault against your constancy.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Why then, to say, ‘prove my constancy’, is as much as to say, ‘kiss me’.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Most true, rare lady.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Then prove my constancy.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Believe me, madam, you gather exceeding wittily upon it.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Oh my forehead, my very heart aches at a blow! [Aloud] What dost thou mean, wife? Thou wilt lose thy fame, discredit thy religion, and dishonour me forever.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Away, sir, I will abide no more of your proof, nor endure any more of your trial.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Oh, she dares not, she dares not. I am as glad I have tried your purity as may be. You, the most constant lady in France? I know an hundred ladies in this town that will dance, revel all night amongst gallants, and in the morning go to bed to her husband as clear a woman as if she were new christened, kiss him, embrace him, and say, ‘no, no, husband, thou art the man’, and he takes her for the woman.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: And all this can I do.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Take heed of it, wife.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Fear not, my good head, I warrant you, for him.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Nay, madam, triumph not before the victory. How can you conquer that against which you never strive, or strive against that which never encounters you? To live idle in this walk, to enjoy this company, to wear this habit, and have no more delights than those will afford you, is to make Virtue an idle housewife, and to hide herself in slothful cobwebs that still should be adorned with actions of victory. No, madam, if you will unworthily prove your constancy to your husband, you must put on rich apparel, fare daintily, hear music, read sonnets, be continually courted, kiss, dance, feast, revel all night amongst gallants. Then if you come to bed to your husband with a clear mind and a clear body, then are your virtues ipsissima , then have you passed the full test of experiment, and you shall have an hundred gallants fight thus far in blood for the defence of your reputation.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: O vanity of vanities!

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Oh husband, this is perfect trial indeed.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: And you will try all this now, will you not?

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Yea, my good head, for it is written, we must pass to perfection through all temptation, Habbakuk the fourth.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Habbakuk? Cuck me no cucks! In a’ doors, I say. Thieves, Puritans, murderers! In a’ doors, I say.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: So now is he stark mad, i’faith. But, sirrah, as this is an old lord jealous of his young wife, so is ancient Countess Moren jealous of her young husband. We’ll thither to have some sport, i’faith.

div2.head: [Scene 5]
div2.stage: Enter Labesha hanging upon Martia’s sleeve, and the Lord Moren comes to them.

lg.l: I prithee, Besha, keep a little off.
Hang not upon her shoulders thus for shame.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: My Lord, pardonnez-moi , I must not let her talk alone with anyone, for her father gave me charge.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Oh, you are a goodly charger for a goose.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: A goose! You are a gander to call me goose. I am a Christian gentleman as well as you.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Well, sirrah, get you hence, or by my troth I’ll have thee taken out in a blanket, tossed from forth our hearing.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: In a blanket? What, do you make a puppy of me? By skies and stones, I will go and tell your lady.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Nay, but Besha —

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Nay, he will tell, my lord.

div2.stage: Enter the Countess Moren and Labesha.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Why, how now, my lord. What, thought you I was dead, that you are wooing of another thus, or are you laying plots to work my death?

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Why neither, sweet bird. What need you move these questions unto me, whom you know loves you above all the women in the world?

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: How he can flatter now he hath made a fault.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: He can do little, an he cannot cog.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Out, you ass.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Well, come tell me what you did entreat.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Nothing, by heaven, sweet bird, I swear, but to entreat her love —

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: But to entreat her love!

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Nay, hear me out.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Nay here you are out. You are out too much, methinks, and put me in —

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: And put you in?

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: In a fair taking, sir, I mean.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Oh, you may see what hasty taking is. You women evermore scramble for our words, and never take them mannerly from our mouths.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Come, tell me what you did entreat.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: I did entreat her love to Colinet.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: To Colinet? Oh, he is your dear cousin, and your kind heart, i’faith, is never well but when you are doing good for every man. Speak, do you love me?

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: I’faith, sweet bird.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Best of all others?

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Best of all others.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: That’s my good bird, i’faith.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Oh, mistress, will you love me so?

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: No, by my troth, will I not.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: ‘No, by my troth, will I not’? Why, that’s well said. I could never get her to flatter me yet.

div2.stage: Enter Lemot, Blanvel, and Catalian, and Colinet.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Good morrow, my good lord, and these passing lovely ladies.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: So now we shall have all manner of flattering with Monsieur Lemot.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: You are all manner of ways deceived, madam, for I am so far from flattering you, that I do not a whit praise you.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Why do you call us passing lovely then?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Because you are passing from your loveliness.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Madam, we shall not have one mot of Monsieur Lemot, but it shall be as it were a moat to drown all our conceit in admiration.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: See what a mote her quick eye can spy in mine, before she looks in it.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: So mote I thee, thine answer is as good as mought be.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Here’s a poor name run out of breath quickly.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Why, Monsieur Lemot, your name is run out of breath at every word you speak.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: That’s because my name signifies ‘word’.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Well hit, Monsieur Verbum .

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: What, are you good at Latin, lady?

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: No, sir, but I know what verbum is.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, ’tis green bum: vert is green, and you know what bum is, I am sure of that.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: No, sir, ’tis a verb, and I can decline you.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: That you can, I’ll be sworn.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: What can I do?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Decline me, or take me a hole lower, as the proverb is.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Nay, sir, I mean plain grammatical declination.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well, let’s hear your scholarship, and decline me.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: I will, sir, moto, motas .

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Oh excellent! She hath called him ass in Latin.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well, sir, forward.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Nay, there’s enough to try both our scholarships

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Moto, motas . Nay, faith, forward to motavi , or motandi .

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Nay, sir, I’ll leave when I am well.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Why, Monsieur Lemot, your name being in word general, is in ninny, or in hammer, or in cock, or in buzzard.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Or in wagtail, or in woodcock, or in dotterel, or in dizzard.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Or in clot, or in head, or in cow, or in baby.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Or in malkin, or in trash, or in pap, or in lady.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Or, indeed, in everything.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, then ’tis in thing.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Then, good Monsieur Thing, there let it rest.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Then, above all things, I must have a word with you.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Hands off, sir, she is not for your mowing.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: She is for your mocking.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: An she mock me, I’ll tell her father.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: That’s a good child, thou smellest of the mother, and she was a fool, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Meddle with me, but do not meddle with my mother.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: That’s a good child. [To Martia] Come, I must needs have a word with you.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: You shall do none of your needs with her, sir.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Why, what will you do?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: What will I do? You shall see what I’ll do.

div2.stage: Then he offereth to draw [his sword].

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Go to, you ass! Offer to draw here, and we’ll draw thee out of the house by the heels.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: What, three against one? Now was ever proper hard-favoured gentleman so abused? Go to, Mistress Martia, I see you well enough. Are you not ashamed to stand talking alone with such a one as he?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: How, sir? With such a one as I, sir?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Yea, sir, with such a one as you, sir.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, what am I?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: What are you, sir? Why, I know you well enough.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Sirrah, tell me what you know me for, or else by heaven I’ll make thee better thou hadst never known how to speak.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Why, sir, if you will needs know, I know you for an honourable gentleman and the King’s minion, and were it not to you, there’s ne’er a gentleman in Paris should have had her out of my hands.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: Nay, he’s as tall a gentleman of his hands as any is in Paris.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: There’s a favour for you, sir.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: But I can get no favour for you, sir.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: I pray, my lord, entreat for your cousin Colinet.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Alas, man, I dare not for my wife.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Why, my lord, she thinks it is for nothing, but to speak for your cousin.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: I pray you, bird, give me leave to speak for my cousin.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: I am content for him.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Then one word with you more, courteous Lady Martia.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Not an you were my father!

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Gentlemen, for God’s sake thrust this ass out of the doors.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Nay, by’rlady, he’ll run home and tell her father.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Well, go to her. I warrant he shall not trouble you. [To Labesha] Kind gentleman, how we dote on thee. Embrace him, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Oh, sweet Besha, how we honour thee.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Nay gentlemen, look what a piercing eye he hath.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: An eye? I have an eye an it were a pole-cat.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Nay, look what a nose he hath.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: My nose is neat crimson.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Nay, look what a handsome man he is. O Nature, Nature,

lg.l: Thou never madest man of so pure a feature.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Truly, truly, gentlemen, I do not deserve this kindness.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Oh lord, sir, you are too modest. Come shall we walk?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Whither? To the alehouse?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Hark you, madam, have you no more care of the right of your husband, than to let him talk thus affectionately with another?

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Why, he speaks not for himself, but for his cousin Colinet.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: God’s my life! He tells you so. Nay, an these excuses may serve I have done.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: By the mass, now I observe him, he looks very suspiciously indeed. Ne’er trust me if his lookes and his gesture do not plainly show himself to swear, ‘By this light, I do love thee’.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: By’rlady, madam, you guess shrewdly indeed. But hark you, madam, I pray let not me be the author of discord between my good lord and you.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: No, no, Monsieur Lemot, I were blind if I could not see this. I’ll slit her nose, by Jesus.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: How now, what’s the matter?

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: What’s the matter? If I could come at your mistress, she should know what’s the matter.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: My mistress?

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Yea, your mistress. Oh, here’s fair dissimulation! [To Martia] Oh, ye impudent gossip, do I send for you to my house to make you my companion, and do you use me thus? Little dost thou know what ’tis to love a man truly, for if thou didst, thou wouldst be ashamed to wrong me so.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: You wrong me, madam, to say I wrong you.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Go to, get you out of my house.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: I am gone, madam.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Well, come in, sweet bird and I’ll persuade thee there’s no harm done.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Well, we shall hear your persuasions.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well, God knows and I can partly guess what he must do to persuade her. Well, take your fair charge, fair and manly Lord Monsieur Labesha.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: One word with you more, fair lady.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Not a word. No man on pain of death, not a word. He comes upon my rapier’s point, that comes within forty foot on her.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Thanks, good Lemot, and thanks gentlemen all, and her father shall thank you.

sp.speaker: COLINET
sp.p: Much good do it you, sir. Come, gentlemen, let’s go wait upon the King, and see the humour of the young Lord Dowsecer.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Excuse me to the King, and tell him I will meet him there. [Exeunt Colinet, Catalian and Blanvel.] So, this is but the beginning of sport between this fine lord and his old lady. But this wench Martia hath happy stars reigned at the disposition of her beauty, for the King himself doth mightily dote on her. Now to my Puritan, and see if I can make up my full proof of her.

div2.head: [Scene 6]
div2.stage: Enter [Florila] the Puritan in her best attire.

lg.l: Now am I up and ready. Ready? Why?
Because my clothes once on, that call we ready.
But readiness I hope hath reference
To some fit action for our several state.
For when I am attired thus, countess-like,
’Tis not to work, for that befits me not.
’Tis on some pleasure, whose chief object is
One man’s content, and he my husband is.
But what need I thus be attired,
For that he would be pleased with meaner weed?
Besides, I take no pleasure thus to please him
I am content, because it is my duty
To keep to him, and not to seek no further.
But if that pleasure be a thing that makes
The time seem short, if it do laughter cause,
If it procure the tongue but heartily
To say, ‘I thank you’, I have no such thing,
Nor can the godliest woman in the world
against her nature please her sense or soul.
She may say, ‘this I will’, or ‘this I will not’.
But what shall she reap hereby?
Comfort in another world, if she will stay till then.

l.seg: Yea, marry, sir, now I must look about.
Now if her desolate prover come again,
Shall I admit him to make farther trial?
I’ll have a dialogue between myself
And manly reason to that special end:
‘Reason, shall I endure a desolate man to come
And court my wife, and prove her constancy?’
Reason: ‘To court and prove her you may bear, my lord,
For perfect things are not the worse for trial.
Gold will not turn to dross for deepest trial’.
Thanks, gentle Reason, I’ll trouble you no more.

lg.l: [Aloud] God save, sweet wife. Look up, thy tempter comes.
Let him, my lord. I hope I am more blessed
Than to relent in thought of lewd suggestion.
But if by frailty you should yield in thought,
What will you do?
Then shall you keep me close,
And never let me see man but your self.
If not, then boldly may I go abroad.
But how shall I know whether you yield or no?
Hear us yourself, my lord.
Tut, that were gross,
For no woman will yield in her husband’s hearing.
Then to assure you if I yield or no,
Mark but these signs: as he is proving me,
If I do yield, you shall perceive my face
Blush and look pale, and put on heavy looks.
If I resist, I will triumph, and smile,
And when I hold but up my finger,
Stop his vain lips, or thrust him on the breast,
Then is he overthrown both horse and foot.
Why, this doth satisfy me mightily.
See, he is come.
Honour to my good lord and his fair young lady.
Now, Monsieur Satan, you are come to tempt
And prove at full the spirit of my wife.
I am, my lord, but vainly, I suppose.
You see she dares put on this brave attire,
Fit with the fashion, which you think serves much
To lead a woman into light desires.
My lord, I see it, and the sight thereof
Doth half dismay me to make further proof.
Nay, prove her, prove her, sir, and spare not.
What, doth the witty minion of our King
Think any dame in France will say him nay?
But prove her, prove her, sir, and spare not.
Well, sir, though half discouraged in my coming,
Yet I’ll go forward. Lady, by your leave.
Now, sir, your cunning in a lady’s proof.
Madam, in proving you I find no proof
Against your piercing glancings,
But swear I am shot thorough with your love.
I do believe you. Who will swear he loves
To get the thing he loves not? If he love,
What needs more perfect trial?
Most true rare lady.
Then are we fitly met. I love you too.
Exceeding excellent.
Nay, I know you will applaud me in this course.
But to let common circumstances pass,
Let us be familiar.
Dear life, you ravish my conceit with joy.

l.seg: I long to see the signs that she will make.

lg.l: I told my husband I would make these signs:
If I resisted, first, hold up my finger,
As if I said, ‘i’faith, sir, you are gone’,
But it shall say, ‘i’faith, sir, we are one’.

l.seg: Now she triumphs and points to heaven, I warrant you.

lg.l: Then must I seem as if I would hear no more
And stop your vain lips.
Go, cruel lips, you have bewitched me, go.

l.seg: His scornèd words and rates him for his pains.

lg.l: And when I thrust you thus against the breast,
Then are you overthrown both horse and foot.

l.seg: Now is he overthrown both horse and foot.

lg.l: [Aloud] Away, vain man, have I not answered you?
Madam, I yield and swear I never saw
So constant nor so virtuous a lady.
[To Lemot] Now, speak, I pray, and speak but truly,
Have you not got a wrong sow by the ear?
My lord, my labour is not altogether lost,
For now I find that which I never thought.
Ah, sirrah, is the edge of your steel wit
Rebated then against her adamant?
It is, my lord. Yet one word more, fair lady.

p.seg: Fain would he have it do, and it will not be.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Lend him my handkerchief to wipe his lips of their last disgrace.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Excellent good. Go forward, sir, I pray.

lg.l: [To Lemot] Another sign, i’faith, love, is required.
Let him have signs enough, my heavenly love.
Then know there is a private meeting
This day at Verone’s ordinary,
Where if you will do me the grace to come,
And bring the beauteous Martia with you,
I will provide a fair and private room,
Where you shall be unseen of any man,
Only of me, and of the King himself,
Whom I will cause to honour your repair
With his high presence,
And there with music and quick revellings
You may revive your spirits so long time dulled.
I’ll send for Martia then, and meet you there,
And tell my husband I will lock myself
In my close walk till supper-time.
[Aloud] We pray, sir, wipe your lips of the disgrace
They took in their last labour.
[Going] Marry, the Devil was never so despited.
Nay, stay, sir.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: No, no, my Lord, you have the constantest wife that ever — well, I’ll say no more.

lg.l: Never was minion so disminionèd.
Come, constancy, come, my girl, I’ll leave thee
Loose to twenty of them, i’faith.
Come, my good head, come.

div2.head: [Scene 7]
div2.stage: Enter the King and all the lords [Lemot and Catalian], with the trumpets.

lg.l: Why sound these trumpets, in the Devil’s name?
To show the King comes.
To show the King comes?
Go hang the trumpeters. They mock me boldly,
And every other thing that makes me known,
Not telling what I am, but what I seem:
A king of clouts, a scarecrow, full of cobwebs,
Spiders and earwigs, that sets jackdaw’s long tongue
In my bosom and upon my head.
And such are all the affections of love
Swarming in me, without command or reason.
How now, my liege! What, quagmired in philosophy,
Bound with love’s whipcord, and quite robbed of reason?
And I’ll give you a receipt for this presently.
Peace, Lemot. They say the young Lord Dowsecer
Is rarely learned, and nothing lunatic
As men suppose,
But hateth company and worldly trash.
The judgement and the just contempt of them
Have in reason arguments that break affection,
As the most sacred poets write, and still the roughest wind.
And his rare humour come we now to hear.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Yea, but hark you, my liege, I’ll tell you a better humour than that. Here presently will be your fair love, Martia, to see his humour, and from thence, fair countess Florila and she will go unto Verone's ordinary, where none but you and I and Count Moren will be most merry.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Why, Count Moren, I hope, dares not adventure into any woman’s company but his wife’s.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Yes, as I will work, my liege, and then let me alone to keep him there till his wife comes.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: That will be royal sport. (Enter Labervele, Labesha, and all the rest [the Countess, Moren, Foyes, Martia and Florila].) See where all comes. Welcome, fair lords and ladies.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: My liege, you are welcome to my poor house.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: [Presenting Labesha] I pray, my liege, know this gentleman especially. He is a gentleman born, I can tell you.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: With all my heart. What might I call your name?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Monsieur Labesha, Seigneur de Foulasa.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: De Foulasa? An ill-sounding baronry, of my word. But to the purpose. Lord Labervele, we are come to see the humour of your rare son, which by some means I pray let us partake.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Your highness shall too unworthily partake the sight which I with grief and tears daily behold, seeing in him the end of my poor house.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: You know not that, my lord. Your wife is young, and he perhaps hereafter may be moved to more society.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Would to God he would, that we might do to your crown of France more worthy and more acceptable service.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Thanks, good my lord. See where he appears. (Enter Lavel with a picture, and a pair of large hose, and a codpiece, and a sword.) Say, Lavel, where is your friend, the young Lord Dowsecer?

sp.speaker: LAVEL
sp.p: I look, my liege, he will be here anon, but then I must entreat your majesty and all the rest to stand unseen, for he as yet will brook no company.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: We will stand close, Lavel, but wherefore bring you this apparel, that picture, and that sword?

sp.speaker: LAVEL
sp.p: To put him, by the sight of them, in mind of their brave states that use them, or that at the least of the true use they should be put unto.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Indeed, the sense doth still stir up the soul, and though these objects do not work, yet it is very probable in time she may. At least, we shall discern his humour of them.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: See where he comes contemplating. Stand close.

sp.speaker: DOWSECER
sp.p: Quid ei potest videri magnum in rebus humanis cui aeternitas omnis totiusque nota sit mundi magnitudo .

lg.l: ‘What can seem strange to him on earthly things
To whom the whole course of eternity,
And the round compass of the world is known?’
A speech divine, but yet I marvel much
How it should spring from thee, Mark Cicero,
That sold for glory the sweet peace of life,
And made a torment of rich nature’s work,
Wearing thyself by watchful candle-light,
When all the smiths and weavers were at rest,
And yet was gallant, ere the day bird sung,
To have a troop of clients at thy gates,
Armed with religious supplications,
Such as would make stern Minos laugh to read.
Look on our lawyers’ bills: not one contains
Virtue or honest drifts, but snares, snares, snares.
For acorns now no more are in request;
But when the oak’s poor fruit did nourish men,
Men were like oaks of body, tough, and strong.
Men were like giants then, but pygmies now,
Yet full of villainies as their skin can hold.
How like you this humour, my liege?
This is no humour; this is but perfect judgement.
Is this a frenzy?
Oh were all men such,
Men were no men but gods, this earth a heaven.
[Noticing the sword] See, see, the shameless world,
That dares present her mortal enemy
With these gross ensigns of her lenity,
Iron and steel, uncharitable stuff,
Good spital-founders, enemies to whole skins,
As if there were not ways enough to die
By natural and casual accidents,
Diseases, surfeits, brave carouses,
Old aqua-vitae , and too base wines,
And thousands more. Hence with this art of murder!
But here is goodly gear, the soul of man,
For ’tis his better part. Take away this,
And take away their merits and their spirits.
Scarce dare they come in any public view
Without this countenance-giver,
And some dares not come, because they have it, too,
For they may sing, in written books they find it.
What is it then, the fashion or the cost?
The cost doth match, but yet the fashion more,
For let it be but mean, so in the fashion,
And ’tis most gentleman-like. Is it so?
Make a hand in the margin, and burn the book,
A large hose and a codpiece makes a man.
A codpiece, nay indeed, but hose must down.
Well for your gentle forgers of men,
And for you come to wrest me into fashion,
I’ll wear you thus, and sit upon the matter.
And so he doth despise our purposes.
Bear with him yet, my lord, he is not resolved.
I would not have my friend mock worthy men,
For the vain pride of some that are not so.
I do not here deride difference of states,
No, not in show, but wish that such as want show
Might not be scorned with ignorant Turkish pride,
Being pompous in apparel and in mind
Nor would I have with imitated shapes
Men make their native land the land of apes,
Living like strangers when they be at home,
And so perhaps bear strange hearts to their home;
Nor look a-snuff like a piannet’s tail,
For nothing but their curls and formal locks,
When, like to cream bowls, all their virtues swim
In their set faces, all their in-parts then
Fit to serve peasants or make curds for daws.
[Noticing the picture] But what a stock am I thus to neglect
This figure of man’s comfort, this rare piece?
Heavens grant that make him more humane, and sociable.
Nay, he’s more humane than all we are.
I fear he will be too sharp to that sweet sex.
She is very fair. I think that she be painted.
An if she be, sir, she might ask of me,
‘How many is there of our sex that are not?’
’Tis a sharp question. Marry and I think
They have small skill. If they were all of painting,
’Twere safer dealing with them. And indeed.
Were their minds strong enough to guide their bodies,
Their beauteous deeds should match with their heavenly looks,
’Twere necessary they should wear them.
An would they vouchsafe it, even I
Would joy in their society.
And who would not die with such a man?
But to admire them as our gallants do,
‘Oh, what an eye she hath! Oh, dainty hand!
Rare foot and leg!’ and leave the mind respectless.
This is a plague that, in both men and women,
Make such pollution of our earthly being.
Well, I will practise yet to court this piece.
Oh, happy man, now have I hope in her.
Methinks I could endure him days and nights.

sp.speaker: DOWSECER
sp.p: Well, sir, now thus must I do, sir, ere it come to women. ‘Now, sir’ — a plague upon it, ’tis so ridiculous I can no further. What poor ass was it that set this in my way? Now if my father should be the man — [Sees Labervele] God’s precious coals, ’tis he!

lg.l: Good son, go forward in this gentle humour.
Observe this picture. It presents a maid
Of noble birth and excellent of parts,
Whom for our house and honour sake, I wish
Thou wouldst confess to marry.
To marry father? Why, we shall have children.
Why, that’s the end of marriage, and the joy of men.
Oh, how you are deceived. You have but me,
And what a trouble am I to your joy!
But, father, if you long to have some fruit of me,
See, father, I will creep into this stubborn earth
And mix my flesh with it, and they shall breed grass
To fat oxen, asses and such-like,
And when they in the grass the spring converts
Into beasts’ nourishment,
Then comes the fruit of this my body forth.
Then may you well say,
Seeing my race is so profitably increased,
That good fat ox and that same large-eared ass
Are my son’s sons, that calf with a white face
Is his fair daughter, with which, when your fields
Are richly filled, then will my race content you.
But for the joys of children, tush, ’tis gone.
Children will not deserve, nor parents take it.
Wealth is the only father and the child,
And but in wealth no man hath any joy.
Some course, dear son, take for thy honour sake.
Then, father, here’s a most excellent corse.
This is some comfort yet.
If you will straight be gone and leave me here,
I’ll stand as quietly as any lamb,
And trouble none of you.
An hapless man.
How like you this humour yet, my liege?
As of a holy fury, not a frenzy.
See, see, my liege, he hath seen us sure.
Nay, look how he views Martia and makes him fine.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Yea, my liege, and she, as I hope well observed, hath uttered many kind conceits of hers.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Well, I’ll be gone, and when she comes to Verone’s ordinary, I’ll have her taken to my custody.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I’ll stay, my liege, and see the event of this.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Do so, Lemot.

lg.l: What have I seen? How am I burnt to dust
With a new sun, and made a novel phoenix!
Is she a woman that objects this sight,
Able to work the chaos of the world
Into gestion? O divine aspect,
The excellent disposer of the mind
Shines in thy beauty, and thou hast not changed
My soul to sense, but sense unto my soul,
And I desire thy pure society,
But even as angels do to angels fly.
Fly soul and follow him.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: I marvel much at my son’s sudden strange behaviour.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Bear with him yet, my lord, ’tis but his humour. Come. What, shall we go to Verone’s ordinary?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Yea, for God’s sake, for I am passing hungry.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Yea, come, Monsieur Lemot, will you walk?

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: What, will you go?

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Yea, sweet bird, I have promised so.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Go to, you shall not go and leave me alone.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: For one meal, gentle bird. Verone invites us to buy some jewels he hath brought of late from Italy. I’ll buy the best and bring it thee, so thou wilt let me go.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Well said, flattering Fabian. But tell me, then, what ladies will be there?

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Ladies? Why, none.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: No ladies use to come to ordinaries, madam.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Go to, bird, tell me now the very truth.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: None of mine honour, bird. You never heard that ladies came to ordinaries.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Oh, that’s because I should not go with you.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Why, ’tis not fit you should.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Well, hark you, bird, of my word you shall not go, unless you will swear to me, you will neither court nor kiss a dame in any sort, till you come home again.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Why, I swear I will not.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Go to, by this kiss.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Yea, by this kiss.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: Martia, learn by this when you are a wife.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: I like the kissing well.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: My lord, I’ll leave you. Your son Dowsecer hath made me melancholy with his humour, and I’ll go lock myself in my close walk till supper-time.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: What, and not dine today?

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: No, my good head. Come, Martia, you and I will fast together.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: With all my heart, madam.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Well, gentlemen, I’ll go see my son.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: By’rlady, gentlemen, I’ll go home to dinner.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Home to dinner? By’rlord, but you shall not. You shall go with us to the ordinary, where you shall meet gentlemen of so good carriage and passing complements it will do your heart good to see them. Why, you never saw the best sort of gentlemen if not at ordinaries.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: I promise you that’s rare, my lord. And, Monsieur Lemot, I’ll meet you there presently.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: We’ll expect your coming.

div2.head: [Scene 8]
div2.stage: Enter Verone with his napkin upon his shoulder, and his man Jaques with another, and his son [Boy] bringing in cloth and napkins.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Come on, my masters, shadow these tables with their white veils, accomplish the court-cupboard, wait diligently today for my credit and your own, that if the meat should chance to be raw, yet your behaviours being neither rude nor raw, may excuse it. Or if the meat should chance to be tough, be you tender over them in your attendance, that the one may bear with the other.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Faith, some of them be so hard to please, finding fault with your cheer and discommending your wine, saying they fare better at Valere’s for half the money.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Besides, if there be any chibols in your napkins, they say your nose or ours have dropped on them, and then they throw them about the house.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: But these be small faults. You may bear with them. Young gentlemen and wild heads will be doing.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: Come, whose wit was it to cover in this room, in the name of God, I trow?

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Why, I hope this room is as fair as the other.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: In your foolish opinion. You might have told a wise body so and kept yourself a fool still.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: I cry you mercy. How bitter you are in your proverbs.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: So bitter I am, sir.

div2.stage: [Jaquena removes the cloth from the table nearest her]

p.seg: Oh, sweet Jaquena, I dare not say I love thee.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Must you control us, you proud baggage, you?

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: Baggage? You are a knave to call me baggage.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: A knave? My master shall know that.

p.seg: I will not see them.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Master, here is your maid uses herself so saucily that one house shall not hold us two long, God willing.

p.seg: Pardon me, sweet Jaquena. I must make an angry face outwardly, though I smile inwardly.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: Say what you will to me, sir.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: [Aloud] Oh, you are a fine gossip. Can I not keep honest servants in my house, but you must control them, you must be their mistress?

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: Why, I did but take up the cloth, because my mistress would have the dinner in another room, and he called me baggage.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: You called me knave and fool, I thank you, small bones.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: Go to, go to, she were wise enough would talk with you.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Go thy ways for the proudest harlotry that ever came in our house.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Let her alone, boy. I have schooled her, I warrant thee. She shall not be my maid long, if I can help it.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: No, I think so, sir. But what, shall I take up the cloth?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: No, let the cloth lie. Hither they’ll come first, I am sure of it. Then if they will dine in the other room, they shall.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: Good morrow, my host. Is nobody come yet?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Your worship is the first, sir.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: I was invited by my cousin, Colinet to see your jewels.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: I thank his worship and yours.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: Here’s a pretty place for an ordinary. I am very sorry I have not used to come to ordinaries.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: I hope we shall have your company hereafter.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: You are very like to.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: Good morrow, my host, good morrow, good Monsieur Rowley.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: Good morrow to you, sir.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: What, are we two the first? Give’s the cards, here. Come, this gentleman and I will go to cards while dinner be ready.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: No, truly, I cannot play at cards.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: How! Not play? Oh, for shame, say not so. How can a young gentleman spend his time but in play and in courting his mistress? Come, use this, lest youth take too much of the other.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: Faith, I cannot play, and yet I care not so much to venture two or three crowns with you.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: Oh, I thought what I should find of you. I pray God I have not met with my match.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: No, trust me, sir, I cannot play.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: Hark you, my host, have you a pipe of good tobacco?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: The best in the town. Boy, dry a leaf.

p.seg: There’s none in the house, sir.
Dry a dock leaf.

div2.stage: [Boy exits and returns with a pipe.]

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: My host, do you know Monsieur Blanvel?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Yea, passing well, sir.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: Why, he was taken learning tricks at old Lucilla’s house, the muster-mistress of all the smock-tearers in Paris, and both the bawd and the pander were carried to the dungeon.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: There was dungeon upon dungeon. But call you her the muster-mistress of all the smock-tearers in Paris?

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: Yea, for she hath them all trained up afore her.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Good morrow, my host; good morrow, gentlemen all.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Good morrow, Monsieur Blanvel. I am glad of your quick delivery.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Delivery? What, didst thou think I was with child?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Yea, of a dungeon.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Why, how knew you that?

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: Why, Berger told us.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Berger, who told you of it?

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: One that I heard, by the Lord.

sp.speaker: BLANVEL
sp.p: Oh, excellent. You are still playing the wag.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Good morrow, gentlemen all; good morrow, good Monsieur Rowley.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: At your service.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I pray, my lord, look what a pretty falling-band he hath. ’Tis pretty fantastical, as I have seen, made with good judgement, great show, and but little cost.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: And so it is, I promise you. Who made it, I pray?

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: I know not, i’faith. I bought it by chance.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: It is a very pretty one; make much of it.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Boy, I prithee call for a coarse napkin. [Exit Boy.] Good morrow, gentlemen. I would you had been at the tennis-court: you should have seen me abeat Monsieur Besan, and I gave him fifteen and all his faults.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Thou didst more for him than ever God will do for thee.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Jaques, I prithee fill me a cup of canary, three parts water.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: You shall have all water, an if it please you.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: Who called for a coarse napkin?

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Marry I, sweetheart. Do you take the pains to bring it yourself? Have at you, by my host’s leave.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: Away, sir, fie, for shame.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Hark you, my host, you must marry this young wench. You do her mighty wrong else.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Oh, sir, you are a merry man.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: Good morrow, gentlemen. You see I am as good as my word.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: You are, sir, and I am very glad of it.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: You are welcome, Monsieur Foyes. [To Labesha] But you are not, no, not you.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: No? Welcome that gentleman, ’tis no matter for me.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: How, sir? No matter for you. By this rush, I am angry with you, as if all our loves protested unto you were dissembled. No matter for you?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Nay, sweet Lemot, be not angry. I did but jest, as I am a gentleman.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Yea, but there’s a difference of jesting. You wrong all our affections in so doing.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Faith and troth, I did not, and I hope sirs you take it not so.

sp.speaker: ALL
sp.p: ‘No matter for me’, ’twas very unkindly said, I must needs say so.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: You see how they love me.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: I do, sir, and I am very glad of it.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: And I hope, Lemot, you are not angry with me still.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: No, faith, I am not so very a fool to be angry with one that cares not for me.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Do not I care for you? Nay, then.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: What, dost thou cry?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Nay, I do not cry, but my stomach waters to think that you should take it so heavily. If I do not wish that I were cut into three pieces, and that these pieces were turned into three black puddings, and that these three black puddings were turned into three of the fairest ladies in the land for your sake, I would I were hanged. What a devil can you have more than my poor heart?

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Well, hark you, Lemot, in good faith you are to blame to put him to this unkindness. I prithee, be friends with him.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well, I am content to put up this unkindness for this once. But while you live take heed of ‘no matter for me’.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Why, is it such a heinous word?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Oh, the heinousest word in the world.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Well, I’ll never speak it more, as I am a gentleman.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: No, I pray do not.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: My lord, will your lordship go to cards?

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Yea, with you, Monsieur Foyes.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: Lemot, will you play?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Pardon, good Monsieur Rowley. If I had any disposition to gaming your company should draw me beforeany man’s here.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: Labesha, what, will you play?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Play, yea, with all my heart. I pray lend me threepence.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: I’ll play no more.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Why, have you won or lost?

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: Faith, I have lost two or three crowns.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Well, to him again, I’ll be your half.

p.seg: Sirrah, dost thou know that same gentleman there?
No, i’faith, what is he?

A very fine gull and a neat reveller, one that’s heir to a great living, yet his father keeps him so short, that his shirts will scant cover the bottom of his belly, for all his gay outside; but the linings be very foul and sweaty, yea, and perhaps lousy, with despising the vain shifts of the world.
But he hath gotten good store of money now, methinks.

Yea, and I wonder of it. Some ancient serving-man of his father’s that hath gotten forty shillings in fifty years upon his great good husbandry, he swearing monstrous oaths to pay him again, and besides to do him a good turn (when God shall hear his prayer for his father) hath lent it him, I warrant you. But, howsoever, we must speak him fair.
Oh, what else!

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: [Aloud] God save sweet Monsieur Rowley. What, lose or win, lose or win?

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: Faith, sir, save myself and lose my money.

p.seg: Why, hark thee, Catalian; I could have told thee before what he would have said.
I do not think so.

No? Thou seest here’s a fine plump of gallants, such as think their wits singular, and their selves rarely accomplished. Yet to show thee how brittle their wits be, I will speak to them severally, and I will tell thee before what they shall answer me.
That’s excellent, let’s see that, i’faith.
Whatsoever I say to Monsieur Rowley, he shall say, ‘Oh, sir, you may see an ill weed grows apace’.
Come, let’s see.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: [Aloud] Now, Monsieur Rowley, methinks you are exceedingly grown since your to Paris.

sp.speaker: ROWLEY
sp.p: Oh, sir, you may see an ill weed grows apace.

p.seg: This is excellent, forward, sir, I pray.

Whatsoe’er I say to Labesha, he shall answer me, ‘Black will bear no other hue’, and that same old Justice, as greedy of a stale proverb, he shall come in the neck of that and say, ‘Black is a pearl in a woman’s eye’.
Yea, much, i’faith.
Look thee, here comes hither Labesha.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Oh, sir, black will bear no other hue.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: Oh, sir, black is a pearl in a woman’s eye.

p.seg: Sirrah Catalian, whatsoe’er I say to Berger that is so busy at cards, he shall answer me, ‘’Sblood, I do not mean to die as long as I can see one alive’.
Come, let us see you.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: [Aloud] Why, Berger, I thought thou hadst been dead. I have not heard thee chide all this while.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: ’Sblood, I do not mean to die as long as I can see one alive.

p.seg: Why, but hark you, Lemot, I hope you cannot make this lord answer so roundly.
Oh, as right as any of them all, and he shall answer me with an old Latin proverb, that is, usus promptos facit .
Once more, let’s see.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: [Aloud] My lord, your lordship could not play at this game very lately, and now methinks you are grown exceeding perfect.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Oh, sir, you may see, usus promptos facit .

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Monsieur Lemot, here is a gentleman and two gentlewomen do desire to speak with you.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: What, are they come? Jaques, convey them into the inward parlour by the inwarde room, and there is a brace of crowns for thy labour, but let nobody know of their being here.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: I warrant you, sir.

p.seg: So, now the sport begins, I shall start the disguised King plaguily. Nay, I shall put the lady that loves me in a monstrous fright when her husband comes and finds her here.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: [To Lemot] The gentleman and the two gentlewomen desires your company.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I’ll come to them presently.

div2.stage: The Boy speaks in Foyes’s ear.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: Gentlemen, I’ll go speak with one, and come to you presently.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: My lord, I would speak a word with your lordship, if it were not for interrupting your game.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: No, I have done, Lemot.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: My lord, there must a couple of ladies dine with us today.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Ladies? God’s my life, I must be gone.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, hark you, my lord, I knew not of their coming, I protest to your lordship, and would you have me turn such fair ladies as these are away?

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Yea, but hark you, Lemot, did not you hear me swear to my wife that I would not tarry if there were any women? I wonder you would suffer any to come there.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, you swore but by a kiss, and kisses are no holy things, you know that.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Why, but hark you, Lemot, indeed I would be very loath to do anything, that, if my wife should know it, should displease her.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Nay, then you are to obsequious. Hark you, let me entreat you, and I’ll tell you in secret, you shall have no worse company than the King’s.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Why, will the King be there?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Yea, though disguised.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Who are the ladies?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: The flowers of Paris, I can tell you: fair countess Florila and the lady Martia.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Monsieur Lemot, the gentleman and the two gentlewomen desire your company.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I’ll come to them straight. But, Jaques, come hither, I prithee. Go to Labesha and tell him that the Countess Florila and the lady Martia be here at thy master’s house, and if it come in question hereafter, deny that thou told him any such thing.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: What, is this all? ’Sblood, I’ll deny it and forswear it too.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: My lord, I’ll go and see the room be neat and fine, and come to you presently.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Yea, but, hark you, Lemot, I prithee take such order that they be not known of any women in the house.

p.seg: Now to his wife go, i’faith!

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Hark you, Monsieur Labesha, I pray let me speak a word with you.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: With all my heart. I pray look to my stake, there’s threepence under the candlestick.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: I pray, sir, do you know the Countess Florila and the Lady Martia?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Do I know the Lady Martia? I knew her before she was borne. Why do you ask me?

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Why, they are both here at my master’s house.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: What, is Mistress Martia at an ordinary?

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Yea, that she is.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: By skies and stones, I’ll go and tell her father.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: What, you are out of breath, methinks, Monsieur Lemot?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: It is no matter, madam, it is spent in your service, that bear your age with your honesty better than an hundred of these nice gallants, and indeed it is a shame for your husband, that, contrary to his oath made to you before dinner, he should be now at the ordinary with that light hussy Martia, which I could not choose but come and tell you. For indeed it is a shame that your motherly care should be so slightly regarded.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Out on thee, strumpet, and accurst and miserable dame!

p.seg: Now to her husband go I.

lg.l: ‘Nothing else’, quoth you. Can there be more?
Oh, wicked man, would he play false
That would so simply vow, and swear his faith,
And would not let me be displeased a minute,
But he would sigh and weep till I were pleased?
I have a knife within that’s razor-sharp,
And I will lay an iron in the fire,
Making it burning hot to mark the strumpet.
But ’twill be cold too, ere I can come thither.
Do something, wretched woman; stays thou here?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: My lord, the room is neat and fine. Will’t please you go in?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Gentlemen, your dinner is ready.

sp.speaker: ALL [BUT VERONE]
sp.p: And we are ready for it.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Jaques, shut the doors. Let nobody come in.

div2.head: [Scene 10]
div2.stage: Enter Labervele, Foyes, Labesha, and the Countess.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: [Knocking at door] Where be these puritans, these murderers? Let me come in here.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: Where is the strumpet?

lg.l: Where is this harlot? Let us come in here.
What shall we do? The streets do wonder at us,
And we do make our shame known to the world.
Let us go and complain us to the King.
Come, Labesha, will you go?
No, no, I scorn to go. No king shall hear my plaint.
I will in silence live a man forlorn,
Mad, and melancholy as a cat
And never more wear hat-band on my hat.
What dost thou mean? Thou must not hang on me.
Oh, good Lord Moren, have me home with you.
You may excuse all to my father for me.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Oh, my lord, be not so rude to leave her now.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Alas, man, an if my wife should see it, I were undone.

lg.l: Pursue them, sirs, and taking Martia from him,
Convey her presently to Valere’s house.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: What villain was it that hath uttered this?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, ’twas even I. I thank you for your gentle terms. You give me villain at the first. I wonder where’s this old doter? What, doth he think we fear him?

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Oh, monstrous man. What, wouldst thou have him take us?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Would I, quoth you? Yea, by my troth would I. I know he is but gone to call the constable or to raise the streets.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: What means the man, trow? Is he mad?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: No, no, I know what I do, I do it of purpose. I long to see him come and rail at you, to call you harlot, and to spurn you too. Oh, you’ll love me a great deal the better. And yet, let him come, and if he touch but one thread of you, I’ll make that thread his poison.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: I know not what to say.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Speak, do you love me?

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Yea, surely do I.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, then have not I reason that love you so dearly as I do, to make you hateful in his sight that I might more freely enjoy you.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Why, let us be gone, my kind Lemot, and not be wondered at in the open streets.

lg.l: I’ll go with you through fire, through death, through hell.
Come, give me your own hand, my own dear heart,
This hand that I adore and reverence,
And loath to have it touch an old man’s bosom.
Oh, let me sweetly kiss it.
Out on thee, wretch. He hath bit me to the bone.
Oh, barbarous cannibal. Now I perceive
Thou wilt make me a mocking-stock to all the world.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Come, come, leave your passions, they cannot move me. My father and my mother died both in a day, and I rung me a peal for them, and they were no sooner brought to the church and laid in their graves, but I fetched me two or three fine capers aloft and took my leave of them, as men do of their mistresses at the ending of a galliard. Beso las manos .

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Oh, brutish nature, how accurst was I ever to endure the sound of this damned voice.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well, an you do not like my humour, I can be but sorry for it. I bit you for good will, an if you accept it, so; if no, go.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Villain, thou didst it in contempt of me.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well, an you take it so, so be it. Hark you, madam, your wisest course is even to become Puritan again. Put off this vain attire, and say, ‘I have despised all, thanks my God. Good husband, I do love thee in the Lord’, and he (good man) will think all this you have done was but to show thou couldst govern the world, and hide thee as a rainbow doth a storm. My dainty wench, go go. What, shall the flattering words of a vain man make you forget your duty to your husband? Away, repent, amend your life. You have discredited your religion forever.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: Well, wretch, for this foul shame thou puttest on me, the curse of all affection light on thee.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Go, Habbakuk, go. Why, this is excellent. I shall shortly become a schoolmaster, to whom men will put their wives to practise. Well, now will I go set the Queen upon the King, and tell her where he is close with his wench. And he that mends my humour, take the spurs. Sit fast, for by heaven, I’ll jerk the horse you ride on.

div2.head: [Scene 11]
div2.stage: Enter [Verone] my host, Catalian, Blanvel, Berger, Jaques, Jaquena, and Boy.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Well, gentlemen, I am utterly undone without your good helps. It is reported that I received certain ladies or gentlewomen into my house. Now, here’s my man, my maid, and my boy. [To them] Now, if you saw any, speak boldly before these gentlemen.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: I saw none, sir.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: Nor I, by my maidenhead.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Nor I, as I am a man.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Well, my host, we’ll go answer for your house at this time, but if at other times you have had wenches, and would not let us know it, we are the less beholding to you.

div2.stage: Exeunt all but [Verone] my host and the gentlemen [Berger and Catalian].

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: Peradventure the more beholding to him, but I lay my life Lemot hath devised some jest. He gave us the slip before dinner.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Well, gentlemen, since we are so fitly met, I’ll tell you an excellent subject for a fit of mirth, an if it be well handled.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: Why, what is it?

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Why man, Labesha is grown marvellous malcontent upon some amorous disposition of his mistress, and you know he loves a mess of cream and a spice-cake with his heart, and I am sure he hath not dined today, and he hath taken on him the humour of the young Lord Dowsecer, and we will set a mess of cream, a spice-cake, and a spoon, as the armour, picture, and apparel was set in the way of Dowsecer, which I doubt not but will work a rare cure upon his melancholy.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Why, this is excellent. I’ll go fetch the cream.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: And I the cake.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: And I the spoon.

div2.stage: Exeunt, and come in again [and put props down].

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: See where he comes, as like the Lord Dowsecer as may be. Now you shall hear him begin with some Latin sentence that he hath remembered ever since he read his accidence.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum . Oh, silly state of things, for things they be that cause this silly state. And what is a thing? A bauble, a toy, that stands men in small stead. (He spies the cream.) But what have we here? What vanities have we here?

p.seg: He is strongly tempted, the Lord strengthen him. See what a vein he hath.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Oh, cruel fortune, and dost thou spit thy spite at my poor life? But oh, sour cream, what thinkest thou that I love thee still? No, no, fair and sweet is my mistress. If thou hadst strawberries and sugar in thee — but it may be thou art set with stale cake to choke me. Well, taste it, and try it, [He starts to eat.] spoonful by spoonful: bitterer and bitterer still. But oh, sour cream, wert thou an onion. Since Fortune set thee for me, I will eat thee, and I will devour thee in spite of Fortune’s spite.

lg.l: Choke I, or burst I, mistress, for thy sake,
To end my life eat I this cream and cake.

p.seg: So he hath done. His melancholy is well eased, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: [Advancing] God’s my life, gentlemen, who hath been at this cream?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Cream, had you cream? Where is your cream? I’ll spend my penny at your cream.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Why, did not you eat this cream?

lg.l: Talk not to me of cream, for such vain meat
I do despise as food. My stomach dies
Drowned in the cream bowls of my mistress’ eyes.
Nay, stay, Labesha.
No, not I, not I.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Oh, he is ashamed, i’faith. But I will tell thee how thou shalt make him mad indeed: say his mistress for love of him hath drowned herself.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: ’Sblood, that will make him hang himself.

div2.head: [Scene 12]
