div2.stage: Enter the Queen, Lemot, and all the rest of the lords [Foyes and Labervele], and the Countess; Lemot’s [right] arm in a scarf.

l.seg: Have at them, i’faith, with a lame counterfeit humour.

lg.l: [Aloud] Ache on, rude arm, I care not for thy pain,
I got it nobly in the King’s defence,
And in the guardiance of my fair Queen’s right.
Oh, tell me, sweet Lemot, how fares the King?
Or what my right was that thou didst defend?
That you shall know when other things are told.
Keep not the Queen too long without her longing.
No, for I tell you it is a dangerous thing.
Little care cruel men how women long.
What, would you have me then put poison in my breath,
And burn the ears of my attentive Queen.
Tell me whate’er it be, I’ll bear it all.
Bear with my rudeness, then, in telling it,
For, alas, you see I can but act it with the left hand.
This is my gesture now.
’Tis well enough.
Yea, well enough, you say
This recompense have I for all my wounds.
Then thus:
The King, enamoured of another lady,
Compares your face to hers, and says that yours
Is fat and flat, and that your nether lip
Was passing big.
Oh, wicked man.
Doth he so suddenly condemn my beauty,
That, when he married me, he thought divine?
Forever blasted be that strumpet’s face,
As all my hopes are blasted, that did change them.
Nay, madam, though he said your face was fat,
And flat, and so forth, yet he liked it best,
And said a perfect beauty should be so.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Oh, did he so? Why, that was right even as it should be.

sp.speaker: FOYES
sp.p: You see now, madam, how much too hasty you were in your griefs.

sp.speaker: QUEEN
sp.p: If he did so esteem of me indeed, happy am I.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: So may your highness be that hath so good a husband, but hell hath no plague to such an one as I.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Indeed, madam, you have a bad husband. Truly, then did the King

lg.l: Grow mightily in love with the other lady,
And swore no king could more enrichèd be,
Than to enjoy so fair a dame as she.
O, monstrous man, and accurst, most miserable dame!
‘But’, says the King, ‘I do enjoy as fair,
And though I love her in all honoured sort,
Yet I'll not wrong my wife for all the world’.
This proves his constancy as firm as brass.
It doth, it doth. Oh, pardon me, my lord,
That I mistake thy royal meaning so.
In heaven your highness lives, but I in hell.
But when he viewed her radiant eyes again,
Blind was he strucken with her fervent beams.
And now, good King, he gropes about in corners,
Void of the cheerful light should guide us all.
Oh, dismal news! What, is my sovereign blind?
Blind as a beetle, madam, that, a while
Hovering aloft, at last in cow-shards fall.
Could her eyes blind him?
Eyes, or what it was, I know not,
But blind I am sure he is as any stone.

sp.speaker: QUEEN
sp.p: Come, bring me to my prince, my lord, that I may lead him. None alive but I may have the honour to direct his feet.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: How lead him, madam? Why, he can go as right as you, or any here, and is not blind of eyesight.

sp.speaker: QUEEN
sp.p: Of what then?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Of reason.

sp.speaker: QUEEN
sp.p: Why, thou saidst he wanted his cheerful light.

lg.l: Of reason still I meant, whose light you know
Should cheerfully guide a worthy king;
For he doth love her, and hath forcèd her
Into a private room where now they are.
What mocking changes is there in thy words,
Fond man. Thou murderest me with these exclaims.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, madam, ’tis your fault. You cut me off before my words be half done.

lg.l: Forth, and unlade the poison of thy tongue.
Another lord did love this curious lady,
Who hearing that the King had forcèd her
As she was walking with another earl,
Ran straightways mad for her, and with a friend
Of his, and two or three black ruffians more,
Broke desperately upon the person of the King,
Swearing to take from him, in traitorous fashion,
The instrument of procreation
With them I fought a while and got this wound,
But being unable to resist so many,
Came straight to you to fetch you to his aid.
Why raised you not the streetes?
That I forbore,
Because I would not have the world to see
What a disgrace my liege was subject to,
Being with a woman in so mean a house.
Whose daughter was it that he forced, I pray?
Your daughter, sir.
Whose son was it that ran so mad for her?
Your son, my lord.
O gods and fiends forbid!
I pray, sir, from whom did he take the lady?
From your good lord.
O Lord, I beseech thee, no!

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: ’Tis all too true. Come, follow the Queen and I where I shall lead you.

lg.l: Oh, wretched Queen, what would they take from him?
The instrument of procreation.

div2.head: [Scene 13]

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Now was there ever man so much accurst that, when his mind misgave him, such a man was hapless to keep him company? Yet who would keep him company but I? O vile Lemot, my wife and I are bound to curse thee while we live, but chiefly I. Well, seek her or seek her not; find her, or find her not, I were as good see how hell opens as look upon her.

div2.stage: Enter Catalian and Berger behind him.

p.seg: We have him, i’faith. Stop thou him there, and I will meet him here.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Well, I will venture once to seek her.

sp.speaker: BERGER
sp.p: God’s lord, my lord! Come you this way? Why, your wife runs ranging like as if she were mad, swearing to slit your nose if she can catch you.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: What shall I do at the sight of her and hern?

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: God’s precious, my lord! Come you this way? Your wife comes ranging with a troop of dames, like Bacchus’ drunken frows, just as you go. Shift for yourself, my lord.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Stay, good Catalian.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: No, not I, my lord.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: How now, Jaques, what’s the news?

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: None but good, my lord.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Why, hast not seen my wife run round about the streets?

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Not I, my lord. I come to you from my master, who would pray you to speak to Lemot, that Lemot might speak to the King, that my master’s lottery for his jewels may go forward. He hath made the rarest device that ever you heard. We have Fortune in it, and she our maid plays, and I and my fellow carry two torches, and our boy goes before and speaks a speech. ’Tis very fine, i’faith, sir.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Sirrah, in this thou mayst highly pleasure me. Let me have thy place to bear a torch, that I may look on my wife, an she not see me. For if I come into her sight abruptly, I were better be hanged.

sp.speaker: JAQUES
sp.p: Oh, sir, you shall, or anything that I can do. I’ll send for your wife too.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: I prithee do.

div2.head: [Scene 14]
div2.stage: Enter the Queen, and all that were in before [Lemot, with arm in sling, Foyes, Labervele and the Countess].

lg.l: This is the house
Where the mad lord did vow to do the deed.
Draw all your swords, courageous gentlemen.
I’ll bring you there where you shall honour win.
But I can tell you, you must break your shin.
Who will not break his neck to save his king?
Set forward, Lemot.
Yea, much good can I do with a wounded arm.
I’ll go and call more help.
Others shall go, nay, we will raise the streets.
Better dishonour than destroy the King.

p.seg: ’Sblood, I know not how to excuse my villainy. I would fain be gone.

lg.l: I’ll geld the adulterous goat, and take from him
The instrument that plays him such sweet music.

l.seg: Oh, rare! This makes my fiction true. Now I’ll stay.

lg.l: Arrest these faithless traitorous gentlemen.
What is the reason that you call us traitors?

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Nay, why do you attempt such violence against the person of the King?

lg.l: Against the King? Why this is strange to me.
How now, my masters? What? Weapons drawn!
Come you to murder me?
How fares my lord?

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: How fare I? Well. [To Lemot] But you, i’faith, shall get me speak for you another time. [To company] He got me here to woo a curious lady, and she tempts him. Say what I can, offer what state I will in your behalf, Lemot, she will not yield.

p.seg: I’faith, my liege, what a hard heart hath she. Well, hark you, I am content your wit shall save your honesty for this once.
Peace, a plague on you, peace.

sp.speaker: QUEEN
sp.p: Because I feared that you were hurt, my lord.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Hurt, how, I pray?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, hurt, madam? I am well again.

sp.speaker: QUEEN
sp.p: Do you ask? Why, he told me Dowsecer and this his friend, threatened to take away —

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: To take away? What should they take away?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Name it, madam.

sp.speaker: QUEEN
sp.p: Nay, I pray, name it you.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why then, thus it was, my liege. I told her Dowsecer, and this his friend, threatened to take away, an if they could, the instrument of procreation. And what was that now but Martia? Being a fair woman, is not she the instrument of procreation, as all women are?

sp.speaker: QUEEN
sp.p: O wicked man!

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Go to, go to, you are one of those fiddles too, i’faith.

lg.l: Well, pardon my minion that hath frayed you thus.
’Twas but to make you merry in the end.
I joy it ends so well, my gracious lord.
But say, my gracious lord, is no harm done
Between my loving daughter and your grace?
No, of my honour and my soul, Foyes.
The fire of love which she hath kindled in me
Being greater than my heat of vanity,
Hath quite expelled —

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Come, Dowsecer, receive with your lost wits your love, thought lost. I know you’ll yield, my lord, and you, her father.

sp.speaker: BOTH [DOWSECER AND FOYES]
sp.p: Most joyfully, my lord.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: And for her part I know her disposition well enough.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: What, will you have her?

sp.speaker: DOWSECER
sp.p: Yea, marry will I.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: I’ll go and tell Labesha presently.

p.seg: Monsieur Lemot, I pray let me speak with you. I come to you from the Lord Moren, who would desire you to speak to the King for my master’s lottery, and he hath my place to bear a torch, for bare-faced he dares not look upon his wife, for his life.
Oh, excellent. I’ll further thy master’s lottery an it be but for this jest only.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: With all my heart. Can you be ready so soon?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Presently, an if it like your grace.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: But hark you, Lemot, how shall we do for every man’s posy?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Will you all trust me with the making of them?

sp.speaker: ALL
sp.p: With all our hearts.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Why, then, I’ll go to make the posies and bring Labesha to the lottery presently.

lg.l: Surely the world is full of vanity.
A woman must take heed she do not hear
A lewd man speak, for every woman cannot
When she is tempted, when the wicked fiend
Gets her into his snares, escape like me.
For grace’s measure is not so filled up,
Nor so pressed down in everyone as me.
But yet I promise you a little more.
Well, I’ll go seek my head, who shall take me in
The gates of his kind arms, untouched of any.
What, madam, are you so pure now?
Yea, would not you be pure?
No, Puritan.
You must be then a devil, I can tell you.
Oh, wife, where hast thou been?
Where did I tell you I would be, I pray.
In thy close walk, thou saidst.
And was I not?

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: Truly, I know not. I neither looked nor knocked, for Labesha told me that you and fair Martia were at Verone’s ordinary.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Labesha? My lord, you are a wise man to believe a fool.

lg.l: Well, my good head, for my part I forgive you.
But surely you do much offend to be
Suspicious: where there is no trust, there is no love,
And where there is no love ’twixt man and wife,
There’s no good dealing surely. For as men
Should ever love their wives, so should they ever trust them.
For what love is there where there is no trust?
She tells you true, my lord.
She doth, my liege. And, dear wife, pardon this,
And I will never be suspicious more.
Why, I say I do.

div2.stage: Enter [Catalian and] Lemot leading Labesha in a halter.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Look you, my liege, I have done simple service amongst you. Here is one had hanged himself for love, thinking his mistress had done so for him. Well, see, your mistress lives.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: And doth my mistress live?

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: She doth, O noble knight, but not your mistress now.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: ’Sblood, but she shall for me, or for nobody else.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: How now. What, a traitor! Draw upon the King!

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Yea, or upon any woman here in a good cause.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Well, sweet Besha, let her marry Dowsecer. I’ll get thee a wife worth fifteen of her. Wilt thou have one that cares not for thee?

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Not I, by the Lord, I scorn her. I’ll have her better if I can get her.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Why, that’s well said.

p.seg: What, madam, are you turned Puritan again?
When was I other, pray?
Marry, I’ll tell you when: when you went to the ordinary, and when you made false signs to your husband, which I could tell him all.
Cursed be he that maketh debate ’twixt man and wife.
O rare scripturian! You have sealed up my lips.

div2.stage: Enter two with torches, the one of them Moren, then [Verone] my host and his son [Boy], then his Maid [Jaquena] dressed like Queen Fortune, with two pots in her hands.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: What is he?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: This is Verone’s son, my liege.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: What shall he do?

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Speak some speech that his father hath made for him.

sp.speaker: QUEEN
sp.p: Why, is he good at speeches?

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Oh, he is rare at speeches.

lg.l: Fair ladies most tender,
And nobles most slender,
And gentles whose wits be scarce —

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: My host, why do you call us ‘nobles most slender’?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: An it shall please your Grace, to be slender is to be proper, and therefore where my boy says ‘nobles most slender’, it is as much to say, fine and proper nobles.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Yea, but why do you call us ‘gentles whose wits are scarce’?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: To be scarce is to be rare, and therefore, whereas he says ‘gentles whose wits be scarce’, is as much as to say, gentles whose wits be rare.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well, forwards, truchman.

lg.l: Fair ladies most tender,
And nobles most slender,
And gentles whose wits be scarce;
Queen Fortune doth come
With her trump and her drum,
As it may appear by my verse.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: [To Verone] Come hither. Are you a schoolmaster? Where was Fortune queen, of what country or kingdom?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Why, sir, Fortune was Queen over all the world.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: That’s a lie: there’s none that ever conquered all the world, but master Alexander. I am sure of that.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: O rare Monsieur Labesha! Who would have thought he could have found so rare a fault in the speech.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: I’ll alter it, if it please your grace.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: No, ’tis very well.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Father, I must begin again. They interrupt me so.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: I beseech your grace, give the boy leave to begin again.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: With all my heart. ’Tis so good we cannot hear it too oft.

lg.l: Fair ladies most tender,
And nobles most slender,
And gentles whose wits are scarce;
Queen Fortune doth come
With her fife and her drum,
As it doth appear by my voice.
Here is Fortune good,
But ill by the rood,
And this naught but good shall do you, sir;
Dealing the lots
Out of our pots,
And so good Fortune to you, sir.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Look you, my liege, how he that carries the torch trembles extremely.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: I warrant ’tis with care to carry his torch well.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Nay, there is something else in the wind. Why, my host, what means thy man Jaques to tremble so?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Hold still, thou knave. What, art thou afraid to look upon the goodly presence of a king? Hold up, for shame.

p.seg: Alas, poor man, he thinks ’tis Jaques his man. Poor lord, how much is he bound to suffer for his wife?

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Hark you, mine host, what goodly person is that? Is it Fortune herself?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: I’ll tell your majesty in secret who it is: it is my maid, Jaquena.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: I promise you she becomes her state rarely.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Well, my liege, you were all content that I should make your posies. Well, here they be, every one. Give Master Verone his five crowns.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: There’s mine and the Queen’s.

sp.speaker: LABERVELE
sp.p: There’s ours.

sp.speaker: DOWSECER
sp.p: And there is mine and Martia’s.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Come, Labesha, thy money.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: You must lend me some, for my boy is run away with my purse.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Thy boy? I never knew any that thou hadst.

sp.speaker: LABESHA
sp.p: Had not I a boy three or four years ago, and he ran away?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: And never since he went thou hadst not a penny? But stand by, I’ll excuse you. But, sirrah Catalian, thou shalt stand on one side and read the prizes, and I will stand on the other and read the posies.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Content, Lemot.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Come on, Queen Fortune, tell every man his posy. This is orderly, the King and Queen are first.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Come, let us see what goodly posies you have given us.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: This is your majesty’s: ‘At the fairest, so it be not Martia’.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: A plague upon you, you are still playing the villain’s with me.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: This is the Queen’s: ‘Obey the Queen’, an she speaks it to her husband, or to Fortune, which she will.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: A prize. Your majesty’s is the sum of four shillings in gold.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Why, how can that be? There is no such coin.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: [Offering gold] Here is the worth of it, if it please your Grace.

lg.l: Well, what’s for me?
A heart of gold.
A goodly jewel.
Count Labervele and Florila.
What’s my posy, sir, I pray?
Marry, this, my Lord:
Of all Fortune’s friends that hath joy in this life,
He is most happy that puts a sure trust in his wife.
A very good one, sir. I thank you for it.
What’s mine I pray?
Marry this, madam:
Good Fortune, be thou my good fortune-bringer,
And make me amends for my poor bitten finger.
Who bit your finger, wife?
Nobody, ’tis vain posy.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Blank for my Lord Labervele; for his wife a posy, a pair of holy beads with a crucifix.

sp.speaker: FLORILA
sp.p: O bomination idol! I’ll none of them.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Keep them thyself, Verone, she will not have them.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Dowsecer and Martia. I have fitted your lordship for a posy.

sp.speaker: DOWSECER
sp.p: Why, what is it?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Ante omnia una .

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: And what is mine, sir?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: A serious one, I warrant you: ‘Change for the better’.

sp.speaker: MARTIA
sp.p: That’s not amiss.

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: A prize! Dowsecer hath a caduceus, or Mercury’s rod of gold, set with jacinths and emeralds.

sp.speaker: DOWSECER
sp.p: What is for Martia?

sp.speaker: CATALIAN
sp.p: Martia hath the two serpents’ heads set with diamonds.

lg.l: What my host Verone?
What, is he in for his own jewels?
Oh, what else, my liege. ’Tis our bounty, and his posy is:
To tell you the truth in words plain and mild,
Verone loves his maid, and she is great with child.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: What, Queen Fortune with child! Shall we have young fortunes, my host?

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: I am abused, an if it please your majesty.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: I’ll play no more.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: No, faith, you need not now, you have played your bellyful already.

sp.speaker: VERONE
sp.p: Stand still, good Jaquena, they do but jest.

sp.speaker: JAQUENA
sp.p: Yea, but I like no such jesting.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Come, great Queen Fortune, let see your posies. [To the Countess] What, madam, alas, your ladyship is one of the last.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: What is my posy, sir, I pray?

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Marry, madam, your posy is made in manner and form of an echo, as if you were seeking your husband, and Fortune should be the echo, and this you say: ‘Where is my husband hid so long unmasked?’ ‘Masked’, says the echo. ‘But in what place, sweet Fortune? Let me hear’. ‘Here’, says the echo.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: There you lie, echo, for if he were here we must needs see him.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Indeed, sweet King, there methinks the echo must needs lie. If he were here, we must needs see him. ’Tis one of them that carries the torches. No, that cannot be neither, and yet, by the mass, here’s Jaques. Why, my host, did not you tell me that Jaques should be a torchbearer? Who is this? [Revealing Moren] God’s my life, my lord!

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: [Trying to leave] An you be gentlemen, let me go.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Nay, come your way, you may be well enough ashamed to show your face that is a perjured wretch. Did not you swear, if there were any wenches at the ordinary, you would straight come home?

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Why, who told you, madam, there were any there?

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: He that will stand to it: Lemot, my liege.

sp.speaker: LEMOT
sp.p: Who? I stand to it? Alas, I told you in kindness and good will, because I would not have you company long from your husband.

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Why, lo you, bird, how much you are deceived.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Why, wherefore were you afraid to be seen?

sp.speaker: MOREN
sp.p: Who? I afraid? Alas, I bore a torch to grace this honourable presence. For nothing else, sweet bird.

lg.l: Thanks, good Moren. See, lady, with what wrong
You have pursued your most enamoured lord.
But come, now all are friends, now is this day
Spent with unhurtful motives of delight,
And overjoys more my senses at the night.
And now for Dowsecer: if all will follow my device,
His beauteous love and he shall married be,
And here I solemnly invite you all
Home to my court, where with feasts we will crown
This mirthful day, and vow it to renown.
